intro: Right now, while you read this, your heart is beating. Your lungs are filling with air. Your stomach may be working on your last meal. Your brain is turning these letters into ideas. You do not have to tell any of these parts what to do. They work on their own, and they work together.

In this unit you will explore the main systems of the body: bones and muscles, the heart and blood, the lungs, digestion, the brain and nerves, and the skin. Then you will learn how food gives these systems the fuel and building blocks they need. You will see healthy meals from many parts of the world.

By the end, you will be able to name the body's main systems and explain how they team up. You will be able to read a food label, use MyPlate and plan a balanced meal. You will also be able to explain why no single food is 'bad,' and why balance and variety help.
bigQuestion: How do the body's systems work together, and how does food help them do their jobs?

timeline.t: Andreas Vesalius publishes careful drawings of the human body, based on his own study.
William Harvey shows that the heart pumps blood around the body in a loop.
James Lind reports his test showing oranges and lemons help sailors with scurvy.
René Laennec invents the stethoscope to listen to the heart and lungs.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays, letting doctors see bones inside the body.
Casimir Funk uses the word 'vitamine' for nutrients needed in small amounts.
Grand Rapids, Michigan, becomes the first U.S. city to add fluoride to its water.
The U.S. National School Lunch Program begins.
The Nutrition Facts label becomes required on most U.S. packaged foods.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture introduces MyPlate.

words.d: the frame of bones inside the body; an adult has 206 bones
body tissue that can squeeze and pull to make movement
a place where two bones meet so the body can bend or turn
the way blood travels in a loop around the body and back to the heart
blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart
two spongy organs in the chest that take in air
the way the body breaks food into tiny parts it can use
thin threads that carry messages between the brain and the body
a body part that does a special job, like the heart, lungs or skin
the things in food that the body needs to grow, move and stay healthy
a nutrient that helps the body build and repair muscles, skin and other parts
eating many different kinds of foods

test.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
test.why: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through the blood vessels.

test.q: What is the largest organ of the body?
test.why: Skin is the largest organ. It protects you and helps keep you cool.

test.q: Which gas do you breathe out as waste?
test.why: The lungs take in oxygen and send out carbon dioxide.

test.q: What ties a muscle to a bone?
test.why: Tendons are strong cords that tie muscles to bones.

test.q: Which body system includes the brain, spinal cord and nerves?
test.why: The brain, spinal cord and nerves carry messages. They form the nervous system.

test.q: When you run, why do you breathe faster?
choices: To bring in more oxygen for your muscles
test.why: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the lungs and heart speed up together.

test.q: Where are most useful parts of food taken into the blood?
test.why: The small intestine is a long, folded tube where food parts pass into the blood.

test.q: Which nutrient is needed in small amounts and was missing for James Lind's sailors?
test.why: Oranges and lemons helped the sailors. They have vitamin C.

test.q: Which food is a good source of calcium?
test.why: Calcium is found in milk, yogurt, tofu and leafy greens. It builds bones and teeth.

test.q: On MyPlate, what does the small cup stand for?
test.why: The cup beside the MyPlate stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt, or fortified soy milk.

test.q: On a food label, 20 percent Daily Value of a nutrient is usually thought of as...
test.why: As a rough guide, 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

test.q: How do germs in the mouth cause cavities?
choices: They use sugar to make acid
test.why: Germs eat sugar and make acid. The acid can make holes in teeth.

test.q: Which meal gives a grain, a protein and a vegetable?
choices: Rice, lentil dal and cooked spinach
test.why: Rice is a grain, lentil dal gives protein and spinach is a vegetable.

choices: That food is digested in the brain
That blood circulates in a loop
test.why: In 1628 Harvey showed that the heart pumps the same blood around the body again and again.

test.q: What does this unit say about 'bad' foods?
choices: Only foods from one country are healthy
No single food is bad; balance and variety matter most
Sweets should be eaten at every meal
test.why: The unit teaches balance and variety. A treat now and then fits in a healthy week.

write.prompt: A friend says, "Food only matters for your stomach." Do you agree? Write a paragraph that answers the question. Use two or three facts from this unit about how food helps other body systems, like muscles, bones, blood or teeth.
tips: Start with a clear sentence that says what you think.
Name at least two nutrients and the body parts they help.
Use unit words, like nutrients, circulation or muscle.
Name where a fact came from, like MyPlate or James Lind's test.
End by telling your friend what helps: balance and variety.

title: How the Body Works

chapters.title: Body Systems Working Together
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the parts of your body work as one team to keep you moving and alive?

story.title: The Last Lap
story.kicker: In the final lap of a race, Maya feels her whole body speed up at once.
paragraphs: Maya stands at the start line of the school track. It is the fourth-grade relay. Her friends cheer from the grass. She will run the last lap. She shakes out her arms and waits for the baton.
The baton slaps into her hand. Maya pushes off. The muscles in her legs pull hard on her bones. Her feet hit the track again and again. Her arms swing to help her balance.
Halfway around, she feels her heart pounding. It is beating much faster now. It sends more blood to her busy legs. Her breath comes quick and deep. Her lungs pull in more air with every step.

Her face feels hot. Small drops of sweat appear on her forehead. Her skin is helping cool her down. Her eyes find the finish line. Her brain sends a message: go, go, go! She crosses the line, smiling and out of breath.
Later, Maya sits on the grass and drinks water. Her heart slows down. Her breathing gets calm again. She did not have to think about any of it. Her body systems worked together as one team.
story.think: Maya's heart, lungs, muscles, skin and brain all changed during the race. Which change do you think helped her the most, and why?

lessons.title: Your Skeleton
lessons.mainIdea: An adult skeleton has 206 bones that hold the body up and protect the soft parts inside.
reading: Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel hard ridges? Those are your ribs. Ribs are part of your *skeleton*. The skeleton is the frame of bones inside your body. An adult has 206 bones.

Babies are born with more bones than adults. Many of their bones are soft at first. As a child grows, some bones join together. That is why a grown-up ends up with 206. The longest bone is the thigh bone, called the femur.

Bones do many jobs. They hold you up, like the frame of a house. They also protect soft parts. Your skull guards your brain. Your ribs guard your heart and lungs. Inside many bones is soft *marrow*, which makes new blood cells.

words.d: the frame of bones inside the body
the soft middle of many bones, where new blood cells are made
the thigh bone, the longest bone in the body

look.title: Counting Bones
look.prompt: Add the bones in both hands and both feet. What share of the 206 bones are in your hands and feet?

check.q: How many bones does an adult skeleton have?
check.why: The reading says an adult has 206 bones. Babies start with more, and some join as they grow.

check.q: Which bone protects the brain?
check.why: The reading says your skull guards your brain. The ribs guard the heart and lungs.

check.q: What does bone marrow make?
check.why: Marrow is the soft middle of many bones. It makes new blood cells.

lessons.title: Muscles Pull
lessons.mainIdea: Muscles move the body by pulling on bones, and many muscles work in pairs.
reading: Bend your arm and make a fist. Feel the top of your arm get firm. That is your biceps *muscle* at work. A muscle is body tissue that can squeeze and pull. You have more than 600 muscles.

Muscles can only pull. They cannot push. So many muscles work in pairs. The biceps pulls to bend your arm. The triceps, on the back of your arm, pulls to straighten it. Strong cords called *tendons* tie muscles to bones.

Some muscles work without you thinking. Your heart is a muscle that never takes a break. Muscles in your stomach squeeze food along. The muscles you choose to move, like the ones in your legs, help you walk, write and play.

words.d: body tissue that can squeeze and pull to make movement
a strong cord that ties a muscle to a bone

look.title: Try It: The Arm Pair
look.text: Rest one hand flat on the top of your other arm. Slowly bend the arm, then straighten it. Now move your hand to the back of the arm and do it again. Notice which side gets firm each time.
look.prompt: Which muscle tightened when you bent your arm? Which tightened when you straightened it? Why do they need to work as a pair?

check.q: Why do many muscles work in pairs?
choices: Muscles need a friend to make blood
Muscles can only pull, not push
check.why: The reading says muscles can only pull. One muscle bends a joint, and its partner pulls it straight again.

check.q: What ties a muscle to a bone?
check.why: Tendons are strong cords that tie muscles to bones.

check.q: Which muscle works without you thinking about it?
choices: Your leg muscles when you kick
Your finger muscles when you write
check.why: The heart is a muscle that works all the time, even while you sleep, without you choosing to move it.

lessons.title: Joints Let You Bend
lessons.mainIdea: Joints are the places where bones meet, and they let the body bend, twist and turn.
reading: Try to pick up a pencil without bending your fingers. It is very hard! Your fingers bend at *joints*. A joint is a place where two bones meet. You have joints in your knees, elbows, hips and neck.

Joints move in different ways. Your elbow and knee work like a door hinge. They bend back and forth. Your shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints. A round end of one bone fits into a cup in another. So your arm can swing in a circle.

The ends of bones at a joint are covered with *cartilage*. Cartilage is smooth and a little bendy. You can feel it in the tip of your nose and your ears. It helps bones slide past each other without rubbing.

words.d: a place where two bones meet so the body can bend or turn
smooth, bendy tissue that covers bone ends and shapes the nose and ears

look.title: Hinge or Ball?
look.text: Swing your arm in a big circle from the shoulder. Now try to swing your lower arm in a circle from the elbow alone. One moves all the way around. One only bends back and forth, like a door.
look.prompt: Which joint is a hinge and which is a ball-and-socket? How can you tell from the way it moves?

check.q: What is a joint?
choices: A cord that ties muscle to bone
A place where two bones meet
The soft middle of a bone
check.why: The reading defines a joint as a place where two bones meet.

check.q: Which joint works like a door hinge?
check.why: The elbow and knee bend back and forth like a hinge. The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints.

check.q: Where can you feel cartilage on your own body?
check.why: The reading says you can feel cartilage in the tip of your nose and your ears.

lessons.title: The Heart Pumps
lessons.mainIdea: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood to every part of the body, all day and all night.
reading: Make a fist. Your *heart* is about the size of your fist. It sits in your chest, a little to the left. The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. Each squeeze is one heartbeat.

For hundreds of years, many people thought blood was made in the liver and used up. In 1628, an English doctor named William Harvey tested this. He measured and watched. He showed that the same blood goes around and around the body. This loop is called *circulation*.
Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day. When you rest, it goes slower. When you run, it speeds up. You can feel the beat in your wrist or neck. That beat is called your *pulse*.

words.d: the muscle in the chest that pumps blood around the body
the way blood travels in a loop around the body and back to the heart
the beat you can feel in your wrist or neck each time the heart pumps

look.title: William Harvey's Discovery
look.text: The blood is pushed by the heart into the arteries, travels through the whole body, and comes back through the veins to the heart. It moves in a circle, again and again, without stopping.
look.cite: William Harvey, On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, 1628 (idea retold in plain words)
look.prompt: What did Harvey say the blood does? How is this different from the old idea that blood was used up?

check.q: About how big is your heart?
choices: About the size of your fist
The size of your whole chest
check.why: The reading says the heart is about the size of your fist.

check.q: What did William Harvey show in 1628?
choices: That the heart is made of bone
That blood is made in the liver and used up
That blood goes around the body in a loop
check.why: Harvey tested the old idea and showed that the same blood circulates around the body again and again.

check.q: What is your pulse?
choices: The beat you feel each time the heart pumps
check.why: The reading says the beat you can feel in your wrist or neck is your pulse.

lessons.title: Roads for Blood
lessons.mainIdea: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny capillaries connect them.
reading: Think of a city with big highways and tiny side streets. Your body has roads for blood. They are called *blood vessels*. Together, the heart and blood vessels make up the circulatory system.

*Arteries* carry blood away from the heart. This blood is full of oxygen, a gas your cells need. *Veins* carry blood back to the heart. You can sometimes see blue lines on your wrist. Those are veins near the skin.

Between arteries and veins are capillaries. Capillaries are so thin that blood cells go through them in single file. There, blood drops off oxygen and food for the cells. It picks up waste to carry away.

words.d: the tubes that carry blood around the body
blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart
blood vessels that carry blood back to the heart
the tiniest blood vessels, where blood trades oxygen and food for waste

look.title: A Trip Through the Roads
look.text: Picture one red blood cell. It leaves the heart on a wide road. The road splits into smaller and smaller streets. At last it squeezes down a tiny lane in your toe. It drops off oxygen there. Then it takes a different road all the way back to the heart.
look.prompt: Name the three kinds of blood vessels the cell traveled through, in order.

check.q: Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?
check.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry it back.

check.q: What happens in the capillaries?
choices: Blood drops off oxygen and picks up waste
check.why: The reading says blood drops off oxygen and food in the capillaries and picks up waste.

check.q: What are the blue lines you may see on your wrist?
check.why: The reading says the blue lines near the skin of your wrist are veins.

lessons.title: Lungs and Breathing
lessons.mainIdea: The lungs bring oxygen into the body and send carbon dioxide out.
reading: Take a slow, deep breath. Feel your chest rise. Air is filling your *lungs*. You have two lungs in your chest. They are soft and spongy. Together with your nose, mouth and windpipe, they form the respiratory system.
A strong, flat muscle sits under your lungs. It is called the *diaphragm*. When it moves down, air rushes in. When it moves up, air goes out. You breathe many times a minute without thinking.

Inside the lungs, air reaches tiny sacs. Oxygen passes from the sacs into the blood. At the same time, a waste gas called *carbon dioxide* leaves the blood. You breathe it out. This trade happens with every breath.

words.d: two spongy organs in the chest that take in air
a flat muscle under the lungs that helps you breathe in and out
a waste gas the body makes and breathes out

look.title: Belly Breathing
look.text: Lie on your back with a small stuffed animal on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Watch the toy rise. Breathe out slowly. Watch it fall. Many people find slow breathing like this helps them feel calm.
look.prompt: Which muscle is moving the toy up and down? What gas goes in, and what gas goes out?

check.q: What is the diaphragm?
choices: A flat muscle under the lungs
check.why: The reading says the diaphragm is a strong, flat muscle under the lungs that helps you breathe.

check.q: Which gas goes from the lungs into the blood?
check.why: Oxygen passes from the air sacs into the blood. Carbon dioxide goes the other way.

check.q: Which body system do the lungs belong to?
check.why: The nose, mouth, windpipe and lungs form the respiratory system.

lessons.title: The Food Journey
lessons.mainIdea: The digestive system breaks food into tiny parts the body can use for energy and growth.
reading: You take a bite of an apple. Your teeth chop it. Your spit, called saliva, makes it soft. Then you swallow. The food slides down a tube called the esophagus. This is the start of *digestion*, the way the body breaks down food.
Next the food lands in your *stomach*. The stomach is a stretchy bag of muscle. It squeezes and mixes food with strong juices. After a few hours, the food is a thick soup.
The soup moves into the *small intestine*. This long, folded tube takes the useful parts into the blood. Then the large intestine takes back water. What the body cannot use leaves as waste.

words.d: the way the body breaks food into tiny parts it can use
a stretchy bag of muscle that mixes food with strong juices
a long, folded tube where food parts pass into the blood

look.title: How Long Is the Food Tube?
look.cite: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), Your Digestive System and How It Works
look.prompt: Which part is longest? Why might a long tube help the body take in more from food?

check.q: What happens to food in the stomach?
choices: It is squeezed and mixed with strong juices
It is sent to the brain
check.why: The reading says the stomach squeezes and mixes food with strong juices.

check.q: Where do useful parts of food pass into the blood?
check.why: The small intestine takes the useful parts of food into the blood.

check.q: What is the esophagus?
choices: The tube food slides down after you swallow
The last part of the intestine
check.why: The reading says the food slides down a tube called the esophagus.

lessons.title: Brain and Nerves
lessons.mainIdea: The brain is the body's control center, and nerves carry its messages to and from every part.
reading: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand back fast. How did that happen so quickly? Your *nerves* did it. Nerves are thin threads that carry messages through your body. They are part of the nervous system.
The *brain* is the control center. It sits inside your skull. It helps you think, remember, feel and move. It also runs things you never notice, like your heartbeat and breathing.

A thick bundle of nerves runs down your back. It is called the *spinal cord*. Your backbone protects it. Messages zoom up the spinal cord to the brain. Answers zoom back down to your muscles, very fast.

words.d: thin threads that carry messages between the brain and the body
the body's control center, inside the skull
a thick bundle of nerves running down the back, protected by the backbone

look.title: The Ruler Catch
look.text: A partner holds a ruler just above your open fingers. Without warning, they let it go. You snap your fingers shut and catch it. Your eyes saw it fall. A message went to your brain. Your brain sent a message to your hand muscles.
look.prompt: Trace the path of the message from your eyes to your fingers. Which body parts carried it?

check.q: What do nerves do?
check.why: The reading says nerves are thin threads that carry messages.

check.q: What protects the spinal cord?
check.why: The spinal cord runs down your back, and your backbone protects it.

check.q: Which job does the brain run without you noticing?
check.why: The reading says the brain also runs things you never notice, like your heartbeat and breathing.

lessons.title: Systems Work Together
lessons.mainIdea: When you run, your muscles, heart, lungs and brain all change together to meet the body's needs.
reading: Think back to Maya's race. Her leg muscles needed more energy. To make energy, muscles need oxygen. So her whole body changed at once. Each group of parts that does a job is called a *body system*.
Her lungs breathed faster to take in more oxygen. Her heart beat faster to carry that oxygen to her legs. Her brain sent messages to keep all of this going. No system worked alone.

When the race ended, her body slowly returned to rest. Keeping things steady inside the body is called *balance*. Your body is always working to keep that balance, whether you are running or sleeping.

words.d: a group of body parts that work together to do one main job
the body keeping things steady inside, like heart rate and temperature

look.title: Before and After
look.text: Sit still and count your breaths for 30 seconds. Then, if it is safe and okay for you, march in place or do jumping jacks for one minute. Count your breaths again. Many students also feel their pulse speed up.
look.prompt: What changed after moving? Which body systems were working together to make that change?

check.q: Why did Maya's heart beat faster during the race?
choices: To carry more oxygen to her muscles
check.why: Her leg muscles needed more oxygen, so her heart beat faster to carry it there.

check.q: What is a body system?
choices: A group of body parts that work together to do one job
check.why: The reading defines a body system as a group of parts that does one main job.

check.q: What does it mean when the body keeps balance?
check.why: In this lesson, balance means the body keeping things steady inside, like heart rate.

lessons.title: Skin, the Largest Organ
lessons.mainIdea: Skin is the body's largest organ; it protects you, helps you feel, and helps keep you cool.
reading: Look at the back of your hand. The skin you see is an *organ*. An organ is a body part that does a special job. Skin is the largest organ of all. On an adult it covers about 20 square feet.
Skin is a shield. It keeps germs and dirt out. It keeps water in. It has nerves that let you feel a soft kitten, a cold ice cube or a sharp pin. It also tells you when something hurts.
Skin also helps control your temperature. When you get hot, you *sweat*. Sweat is salty water that comes out of tiny holes. As it dries, it cools you down. That is what Maya's skin did in the race.

words.d: a body part that does a special job, like the heart, lungs or skin
salty water that comes out of the skin and cools you as it dries

look.title: The Wet Wrist
look.text: Dip a finger in water and wet the inside of your wrist. Blow gently on it. Now blow on your dry wrist. The wet spot feels cooler as the water dries.
look.prompt: How does this show the way sweat helps your body on a hot day?

check.q: What is the largest organ of the body?
check.why: The reading says skin is the largest organ of all.

check.q: How does sweat help the body?
choices: It cools you as it dries
check.why: Sweat is salty water. As it dries on the skin, it cools you down.

check.q: Which is one way skin protects you?
choices: It keeps germs and dirt out
It sends air to the lungs
check.why: The reading says skin is a shield that keeps germs and dirt out.

review.q: Which body system includes the heart and blood vessels?
review.why: The heart and blood vessels together make up the circulatory system.
Muscles can only pull. They pull on bones through tendons.

review.q: Which organ is the body's control center?
review.why: The brain is the control center. It sends messages through the nerves.

review.q: Where does oxygen enter the blood?
review.why: Oxygen passes from tiny air sacs in the lungs into the blood.

review.q: Who showed in 1628 that blood moves in a loop around the body?
review.why: William Harvey, an English doctor, showed that blood circulates.

review.q: In what order does food travel?
review.why: Food starts in the mouth, slides down the esophagus, is mixed in the stomach, then moves to the small intestine.

review.q: An adult has how many bones?
review.why: An adult skeleton has 206 bones. The hand and wrist alone have 27.

review.q: During a race, which change helps cool the body?
review.why: Sweat comes out of the skin and cools the body as it dries.

chapters.title: Food as Fuel
chapters.bigQuestion: How can food from many places give your body what it needs to grow, learn and play?

story.title: Five Lunches, One Table
story.kicker: A class learns that healthy lunches look very different around the world.
paragraphs: Ms. Rivera's fifth-grade class has a new project. Each group gets a photo of a school lunch from another country. Their job is to find out what is on the tray. Then they will compare all five lunches.

Group one has a lunch from Japan. There is rice, a piece of fish, cooked greens and soup. Group two has a lunch from Brazil. There is rice, black beans, a little meat and a salad. The students notice rice in both.

Group three looks at a lunch from India. There is lentil dal, rice, a flatbread and cooked vegetables. Group four has a lunch from China, with noodles and stir-fried vegetables. Group five has a lunch from the United States, with a turkey sandwich, carrots, an apple and milk.

The class lays the photos side by side. Jamal says, "They all look so different." Priya says, "But they all have a grain, a vegetable and something with protein." Ms. Rivera smiles. Priya has found the big idea.
There is no one right lunch for the whole world. Families eat many different foods. Healthy eating is about balance and variety. The class decides to learn what each food gives the body.
story.think: Which of the five lunches would you most like to try? What parts does it share with a lunch you eat at home?

lessons.title: Carbohydrates for Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy, and whole grains give steady energy.
reading: Food gives your body things it needs. These are called *nutrients*. There are six main kinds: carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Each one has its own job.

*Carbohydrates* are your body's main fuel. They are in rice, bread, pasta, tortillas, fruit, beans and potatoes. Your body turns them into a sugar that your cells burn for energy. Your brain uses a lot of it.

Some grains are *whole grains*, like brown rice, oatmeal and whole-wheat bread. They keep the outer part of the grain. That part has fiber. Fiber helps food move through your intestines and helps you feel full longer.

words.d: the things in food that the body needs to grow, move and stay healthy
nutrients in grains, fruits and beans that are the body's main fuel
grains that keep their outer part, like brown rice and oatmeal

look.title: Energy in One Gram
look.cite: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Nutrition Facts label guidance
look.prompt: Which nutrient packs the most energy into one gram? About how many times more than carbohydrate?

check.q: What is the main job of carbohydrates?
check.why: The reading says carbohydrates are the body's main fuel.

check.q: Which food is a whole grain?
check.why: Oatmeal is a whole grain. It keeps the outer part of the grain, which has fiber.

check.q: How does fiber help you?
choices: It helps food move through the intestines
It is a kind of vitamin
It makes the heart beat faster
check.why: The reading says fiber helps food move through your intestines and helps you feel full.

lessons.title: Protein Builds
lessons.mainIdea: Protein helps the body build and repair muscles, skin and other parts.
reading: A scraped knee heals in a week or two. New skin grows over the cut. To build that skin, your body uses *protein*. Protein is a nutrient that builds and repairs body parts.

Protein comes from many foods. Fish, chicken, eggs, milk and meat have protein. So do plant foods like beans, lentils, tofu, peanuts and seeds. Rice and beans together are a protein-rich meal eaten in many countries.
Your muscles, skin, hair and nails are built with protein. Growing children need protein every day. Eating it from different foods is a good way to get enough.

words.d: a nutrient that helps the body build and repair muscles, skin and other parts
small, flat seeds from a plant in the bean family, often cooked into soups and dal

look.title: Protein Hunt
look.text: Look back at the five lunches. Japan had fish. Brazil had black beans and a little meat. India had lentil dal. The United States had turkey and milk. China had noodles and vegetables, and some stir-fries add tofu or egg.
look.prompt: Find the protein on each tray. Which ones come from plants, and which come from animals?

check.q: What does protein do for the body?
choices: It builds and repairs body parts
It is the main fuel for the brain
It keeps water out of the body
check.why: The reading says protein builds and repairs body parts, like new skin over a cut.

check.q: Which is a plant food with protein?
check.why: Lentils, beans, tofu, peanuts and seeds are plant foods with protein.

check.q: Which body parts are built with protein?
check.why: The reading lists muscles, skin, hair and nails as parts built with protein.

lessons.title: Fats Help Too
lessons.mainIdea: The body needs some fat for energy and health, and fats from plants and fish are good choices.
reading: Some people think all fat is bad. That is not true. Your body needs some *fat*. Fat stores energy. It helps your body use some vitamins. It also helps build your brain and nerves.
Fats come in different kinds. Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocados and fish have fats that are good for the heart. These are often called *healthy fats*. Many cooks use them every day.
Butter, cheese and fatty meats have another kind of fat. It is fine in small amounts. Fried snacks and many sweets have a lot of fat and sugar. Doctors say to enjoy them sometimes, not every day.

words.d: a nutrient that stores energy and helps the body use some vitamins
fats from foods like olive oil, nuts, avocados and fish that are good for the heart

look.title: Two Snacks
look.text: Snack A is a handful of peanuts and an orange. Snack B is a bag of fried chips. Both have fat. The peanuts also bring protein. The orange brings vitamins and water.
look.prompt: Which snack gives the body more kinds of nutrients? Is it still okay to enjoy chips sometimes? Explain.

check.q: Which statement about fat is true?
choices: All fat is bad for you
check.why: The reading says your body needs some fat to store energy, use vitamins and build the brain.

check.q: Which food has healthy fats?
check.why: Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocados and fish have fats that are good for the heart.

check.q: What do doctors say about fried snacks and sweets?
choices: Enjoy them sometimes, not every day
They are the best source of protein
check.why: The reading says to enjoy them sometimes, not every day.

lessons.title: Vitamins and Minerals
lessons.mainIdea: Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts, and colorful foods help you get many of them.
reading: Long ago, sailors on long trips got very sick. Their gums bled and they felt weak. In the 1700s, a Scottish doctor named James Lind tested different foods. The sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. Today we know those fruits have *vitamin* C.

Vitamins are nutrients your body needs in small amounts. Vitamin C helps heal cuts. Vitamin A, in carrots and sweet potatoes, helps your eyes. Vitamin D helps your bones. Your skin makes some vitamin D in sunlight.

*Minerals* come from the earth and get into plants and animals. Calcium, in milk, yogurt, tofu and leafy greens, builds strong bones and teeth. Iron, in beans, spinach and meat, helps blood carry oxygen. Eating many colors of fruits and vegetables helps you get many vitamins and minerals.

words.d: a nutrient the body needs in small amounts to work well
nutrients from the earth, like calcium and iron, that the body needs
a mineral that builds strong bones and teeth

look.title: James Lind's Test
look.text: Twelve sailors with scurvy were split into pairs, and each pair was given a different extra food. The two who ate oranges and lemons got better the fastest. One was fit for duty in about six days.
look.cite: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy, 1753 (retold in plain words)
look.prompt: How was Lind's test fair? Why did he give each pair a different food?

check.q: Which fruits helped James Lind's sailors?
check.why: The sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. These fruits have vitamin C.

check.q: Which mineral builds strong bones and teeth?
check.why: The reading says calcium builds strong bones and teeth.

check.q: What is one simple way to get many vitamins and minerals?
choices: Eat many colors of fruits and vegetables
check.why: The reading says eating many colors of fruits and vegetables helps you get many vitamins and minerals.

lessons.title: Water Keeps You Going
lessons.mainIdea: Water is a nutrient too; it makes up much of your body and helps every system work.
reading: After gym class, your mouth feels dry. You head to the drinking fountain. Your body is asking for *water*. Water is one of the six nutrients. You can live much longer without food than without water.
Much of your body is water. It is in your blood, your muscles and even your bones. Water carries nutrients to your cells. It helps you digest food. It helps make sweat to cool you down.

You lose water all day when you breathe, sweat and use the bathroom. So you need to drink more. Plain water and milk are good choices. Fruits like watermelon and oranges have water too. Feeling thirsty is a sign your body needs water; being low on water is called being *dehydrated*.

words.d: a nutrient that carries food to cells, helps digestion and keeps the body cool
when the body does not have enough water

look.title: How Much of You Is Water?
look.cite: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, The Water in You
look.prompt: Who has a higher share of water, a baby or an adult? Which body part on the list has the most?

check.q: What does being dehydrated mean?
choices: Not having enough water in the body
check.why: The reading says being low on water is called being dehydrated.

check.q: Which is one job of water in the body?
choices: It is the body's main fuel
check.why: The reading says water carries nutrients to your cells and helps with digestion and sweat.

check.q: According to the U.S. Geological Survey, about how much of an adult's body is water?
check.why: The data table from the USGS shows an adult body is about 60 percent water.

lessons.title: MyPlate
lessons.mainIdea: MyPlate shows a balanced meal: half fruits and vegetables, plus grains, protein and dairy.
reading: Picture a dinner plate cut into four parts, with a small cup beside it. This picture is called *MyPlate*. The U.S. Department of Agriculture made it in 2011 to help families plan meals.

On MyPlate, fruits and vegetables fill half the plate. Grains fill about a quarter. Protein foods fill the last quarter. The cup stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt. Soy milk with added calcium counts too.

MyPlate is a guide, not a strict rule. It works with foods from any culture. A bowl of rice with fish and greens fits. So do beans, tortillas and salsa. The idea is *balance*: some of each group over the day.

words.d: a U.S. picture guide that shows a balanced meal as a plate with food groups
eating some of each food group, not too much of just one
milk and foods made from milk, like yogurt and cheese

look.title: The MyPlate Message
look.text: Make half your plate fruits and vegetables. Make half your grains whole grains. Vary your protein foods. Move to low-fat or fat-free milk or yogurt, or fortified soy versions.
look.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, MyPlate, 2011 (tips in plain words)
look.prompt: Pick one tip. What is one small change a family could make at dinner to follow it?

check.q: On MyPlate, how much of the plate is fruits and vegetables?
check.why: The reading says fruits and vegetables fill half the plate.

check.q: What does the cup next to the plate stand for?
check.why: The cup stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt, or fortified soy milk.

check.q: Which statement about MyPlate is true?
choices: It only works for American foods
It says to eat just one food group
It works with foods from any culture
check.why: The reading says MyPlate is a guide that works with foods from any culture. It was made in 2011.

lessons.title: Reading a Food Label
lessons.mainIdea: The Nutrition Facts label tells you the serving size and what nutrients are in a packaged food.
reading: Pick up a box of cereal and turn it around. You will find a white box with black letters. It is called the *Nutrition Facts* label. Most packaged foods in the United States must have one.

Start at the top. Find the *serving size*. This is the amount the numbers are about, like one cup. If you eat two cups, you get twice as much of everything. Next, find calories. Calories tell how much energy the food gives.

Then look down the list. You will see fat, sodium, carbohydrates, fiber, sugars and protein. The label also shows added sugars. Added sugars are sugars put in when the food is made. The right side shows a *percent Daily Value*. As a rough guide, 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

words.d: the label on packaged food that lists its nutrients
the amount of food that the label's numbers describe
a number on the label that shows if a food is low or high in a nutrient

look.title: Two Cereals
look.text: Cereal A: serving size 1 cup, 3 grams of fiber, 12 grams of added sugars. Cereal B: serving size 1 cup, 5 grams of fiber, 4 grams of added sugars. Both boxes show the same serving size.
look.prompt: Which cereal has more fiber and fewer added sugars? Why does it matter that the serving sizes are the same?

check.q: What does the serving size tell you?
choices: The amount the label's numbers are about
check.why: The serving size is the amount of food that all the label's numbers describe.

check.q: About what percent Daily Value is thought of as high?
check.why: The reading gives a rough guide: 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

check.q: If you eat two servings, what happens to the numbers?
choices: You get twice as much of everything
check.why: The label's numbers are for one serving. Two servings means twice as much.

lessons.title: Sugar and Your Teeth
lessons.mainIdea: Germs in the mouth use sugar to make acid that can harm teeth, so brushing and fewer sugary drinks help.
reading: Your teeth are covered in *enamel*. Enamel is the hardest part of your body. But tiny germs live in every mouth. When you eat sugar, the germs eat it too. They make acid. Over time, acid can make holes in teeth called *cavities*.

Sticky candy and sugary drinks are hardest on teeth. Soda, sweet tea and juice wash sugar over teeth again and again. Water is a great drink for your teeth. The World Health Organization advises that people keep added sugars low.

You can help your teeth every day. Brush two times a day with fluoride toothpaste. Fluoride is a mineral that makes enamel stronger. See a dentist for checkups. A sweet treat now and then is fine, especially with a meal.

words.d: the hard, shiny outer layer of a tooth
holes in teeth made by acid from germs
a mineral in toothpaste and many water supplies that makes enamel stronger

look.title: Advice on Sugar
look.text: Adults and children should get less than 10 percent of their daily energy from free sugars, which are sugars added to food and drink plus the sugar in honey, syrups and juice. Going below 5 percent may bring even more benefit.
look.cite: World Health Organization, Guideline: Sugars Intake for Adults and Children, 2015 (plain-words summary)
look.prompt: Name two drinks from your week that have free sugars. What could you drink instead?

check.q: What makes cavities in teeth?
choices: Acid made by germs that eat sugar
check.why: The reading says germs eat sugar and make acid, and acid can make holes called cavities.

check.q: What does fluoride do?
check.why: Fluoride is a mineral that makes enamel stronger.

check.q: Which drink is best for your teeth?
check.why: The reading says water is a great drink for your teeth. Sugary drinks wash sugar over teeth.

lessons.title: Healthy Foods Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Families around the world eat many different healthy meals that give the body the same kinds of nutrients.
reading: In Brazil and Mexico, many families eat *rice and beans*. The rice gives carbohydrates. The beans give protein and fiber. Eaten together, they make a filling, healthy meal.

In India, many families eat *dal*. Dal is a warm stew of lentils cooked with spices like turmeric and cumin. It is often served with rice or flatbread. In China, families often stir-fry vegetables in a hot pan with a little oil.

In Japan and many coastal places, people eat a lot of fish. Fish gives protein and healthy fats. Each culture has its own foods. Many of them fit MyPlate well. You can enjoy your family's foods and try new ones too.

words.d: a meal eaten in many countries that gives carbohydrates, protein and fiber
a warm stew of lentils and spices common in India
to cook small pieces of food quickly in a hot pan with a little oil

look.title: Match the Plate
look.text: A plate from Mexico: rice, black beans, grilled chicken, salsa and a slice of avocado. A plate from India: rice, lentil dal, spinach cooked with spices and a spoon of yogurt.
look.prompt: For each plate, find a grain, a protein and a vegetable. What nutrient do the black beans and the lentils both give?

check.q: What is dal?
choices: A kind of noodle from Japan
A warm stew of lentils and spices from India
check.why: The reading says dal is a warm stew of lentils cooked with spices, common in India.

check.q: What do beans give in a rice-and-beans meal?
check.why: The reading says the rice gives carbohydrates and the beans give protein and fiber.

check.q: What does fish give the body?
check.why: The reading says fish gives protein and healthy fats.

lessons.title: Breakfast and Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Breakfast refuels the body for learning, and no single food is 'bad'; balance and variety over the day matter most.
reading: You have not eaten all night. In the morning, your body needs fuel. *Breakfast* breaks that overnight fast. Many students find a good breakfast helps them focus and feel steady in class.

Breakfast can look many ways. Oatmeal with fruit. Eggs and a tortilla. Rice with an egg on top. Yogurt and a banana. Many schools serve free or low-cost breakfast too. A mix of a grain, a protein and a fruit gives lasting energy.

No single food is 'bad.' A piece of birthday cake at a party is fine. What matters is the whole day and the whole week. Eating many kinds of foods is called *variety*. If you have questions about food and your body, ask a parent, school nurse or doctor.

words.d: the first meal of the day, which breaks the overnight fast
eating many different kinds of foods

look.title: Build a Breakfast
look.text: Here are some foods: oatmeal, eggs, tortillas, rice, yogurt, milk, bananas, berries, peanut butter, whole-wheat toast, beans and an orange.
look.prompt: Build two different breakfasts. Each should have a grain, a protein and a fruit. Which one would you like best?

check.q: Why is the first meal called breakfast?
choices: It is eaten at school only
check.why: The reading says breakfast breaks the overnight fast after a night without food.

check.q: What does the lesson say about foods like birthday cake?
choices: No single food is 'bad'; the whole day and week matter
check.why: The lesson says no single food is 'bad.' Balance and variety over time matter most.

check.q: What is variety?
choices: Eating many different kinds of foods
check.why: The reading defines variety as eating many kinds of foods.

review.q: Which of these is one of the six main nutrients?
review.why: The six nutrients are carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

review.q: Which nutrient is the body's main fuel?
review.why: Carbohydrates, in grains, fruit and beans, are the body's main fuel.

review.q: What did James Lind's test with sailors show?
choices: Oranges and lemons helped sailors with scurvy
review.why: Lind found that sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. We now know these have vitamin C.

review.q: On MyPlate, what fills half the plate?
review.why: MyPlate shows fruits and vegetables filling half the plate.

review.q: On a Nutrition Facts label, what should you look at first?
review.why: The serving size tells you the amount all the other numbers describe.

review.q: How is lentil dal like rice and beans?
choices: Both give protein from plant foods
review.why: Lentils and beans are both plant foods in the bean family that give protein and fiber.

review.q: Which habit helps protect teeth from cavities?
choices: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste
review.why: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste makes enamel stronger and helps prevent cavities.

review.q: What is the big idea of healthy eating in this chapter?
choices: Some foods are bad and must never be eaten
Only one country eats healthy food
Balance and variety over the day and week
review.why: The chapter teaches that no food is 'bad' and that balance and variety matter most.
